opus-5.5.text:
I think the way people usually measure the commercial value of users, by daily actives, time spent, or ad impressions, doesn't fully apply to AI products, and sometimes it points you the wrong way.

For a traditional internet product, value mostly comes from attention: the longer someone stays, the more you can monetize them. With an AI assistant, the value comes from how much real work the model does for the user. If someone asks a question and gets a great answer in thirty seconds, that may be a better outcome than an hour of chatting, even though it looks worse on engagement metrics.

So I'd look at a few things.

**The depth of the task.** A user who brings us a fifty-page contract to analyze, a codebase to debug, or a research question that would take a day to work through is very different from someone asking for a joke. The harder and more valuable the task, the more willing they are to pay, and the more the product actually matters in their life.

**Whether it's a habit tied to productivity.** The users I care most about have built the AI into their workflow. They come back because their work depends on it, not because of a notification. That retention is much stickier, and it's where long-term commercial value comes from.

**Feedback into the model.** This is a bit unique to AI. Users with high-quality, real-world tasks help us understand where the model is failing and where its capabilities need to go next. In that sense, their value isn't only revenue. They're part of how the product gets better. A user who pushes the model to its limits is in some ways worth more than ten users who stay well inside its comfort zone.

**Cost structure.** Unlike traditional software, every interaction has a real inference cost. So you can't just say more usage is better. You have to think about the value created per unit of compute. Long term, as models get more efficient and more capable, that equation improves, but right now it's something you have to be honest about.

My overall view is that the biggest commercial value will come from the model's ability to take on more and more of people's real work: first answering questions, then completing longer tasks, eventually acting more like an agent that can carry a project forward. Users' value scales with that. So rather than optimizing hard for traffic numbers today, I think the most important thing is to keep pushing the capability ceiling, because that determines how much value each user can ultimately get, and therefore how much they're worth commercially.

r001.rationale: The response says users bringing demanding work tasks (such as contract analysis, debugging, or research) can matter more commercially than someone asking for a joke, and emphasizes workflow productivity as a source of lasting value.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's still early, and anyone who gives you a precise number is probably guessing. But I'd break it into a few layers.

The first layer is the obvious one: what does a user pay today, either through subscription or through tokens. That's real, but it's the smallest part of the picture, and it can be misleading. Right now a lot of usage is exploratory. People try something, they're curious, and that curiosity doesn't necessarily turn into retention. So if you only look at revenue per user this quarter, you'll overvalue novelty and undervalue the things that actually become habits.

The second layer is time and depth of use. For us, the signal I care about most is whether the product becomes part of someone's workflow, where they come back not because they're interested in AI but because the thing they needed to do got done. A user who spends twenty minutes a day with the model on real work is worth far more than a hundred users who sign up and leave after a weekend. And that depth compounds, because the more context someone gives you, the more the model can do for them, and the harder it is to switch.

The third layer, and this is the one I think people underestimate, is that the value of a user is a function of the model's capability, not a fixed number. As the model gets better, the same user suddenly has more tasks they're willing to hand over. Two years ago maybe you'd let it draft an email. Now you'd let it write code, do research, run through a long multi-step task. The ceiling on what a user is worth keeps moving, because the ceiling on what the model can do keeps moving. So when we think about commercial value, we're really making a bet on the slope of capability improvement, and on whether we can stay close to the frontier.

There's also a question of which users. Developers and knowledge workers are easier to monetize now because the tasks are expensive and the value is legible. A consumer who's chatting casually is harder to price, but the scale is much larger, and I don't think that market has been figured out yet. We'd rather be honest that it's unsolved than pretend we have a formula.

So if you ask me how I assess it, I'd say: look at retention and depth first, be skeptical of early revenue, and remember that the most important variable is one you control, which is how good the model gets.

r001.rationale: The response says developers and knowledge workers are easier to monetize because their tasks are expensive and their value is legible, while casual consumer chat is harder to price. This clearly distinguishes productive professional use as potentially more commercially valuable than casual conversation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to look at how much value the product creates for the user, rather than just counting users. What problem are they solving? How often does that problem arise? And how much better can they solve it with AI?

For example, someone might use a chatbot every day for casual conversation, while another person uses it a few times a week for work that saves them several hours. The second user may have a higher willingness to pay, even though they’re less active. So usage frequency matters, but it isn’t the same as commercial value.

I’d look at retention, willingness to pay, and the cost of serving that user together. With AI, heavy usage also brings inference costs. Ultimately, the question is whether you can consistently deliver enough value that users want to stay and pay, while building a sustainable business around that.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts casual chatbot conversation with work that saves several hours and says the work-focused user may have higher willingness to pay despite using the product less often.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at what problem the product solves for the user, how often that problem comes up, and how much value solving it creates. A user who asks a few casual questions and a user who relies on AI every day for their work may look similar in a registration count, but their willingness to pay can be very different.

So I’d pay attention to retention, depth of use, and whether users are willing to pay—and then consider the cost of serving them. With AI, more usage also brings inference costs, so activity alone doesn’t necessarily translate into commercial value.

But I wouldn’t judge users only by what they pay today. If the product becomes more capable and earns their trust, they may use it for increasingly valuable tasks. The key is whether we can keep delivering enough value that paying for it becomes a natural decision.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts casual questions with daily work use and says willingness to pay may differ, but it does not clearly state that professional, productive use can have greater commercial value.
